treatmentGaps: Build an original flower/bee illustration with an optional field overlay and a clearly illustrative before/after visit; no literal vision, sparks, battery meter, or proven empty-flower detector. Provide static and reduced-motion states.
notes: Science alternate; shares the broader hidden-senses theme with chips but is not the same discovery. Reader novelty untested; Bristol reported extensive contemporary press coverage, so do not label obscure. Retelling hypothesis: a garden has electrical cues humans do not perceive. DOI resolver failed in web tool; the same original paper was opened on a University of São Paulo-hosted mirror. No source figures or datasets copied. Scope limited to the reported laboratory findings, not a current review of all bee electroreception. Full paper body and Fig. 1 caption disagree on the landing sample count (50/51); no sample-count claim or plotted curve is proposed. Do not infer a nectar refill timer or proven avoidance of depleted flowers. No new calculation needed.

entry.title: A flower has another signal
entry.question: What can a bumblebee pick up from a flower besides its colour and smell?
entry.explanation: In a 2013 experiment, bumblebees learned to distinguish artificial flowers by electrical cues. Separate petunia recordings found that a bee visit changed stem potential for about 100 seconds.
entry.qualification: Laboratory results, not proof that bees read a flower’s nectar level. The duration is approximate, not a universal countdown.
entry.whyCare: A garden contains signals our own senses miss.

evidence.scope: Bombus terrestris conditioning and Petunia stem recordings in Clarke et al. (2013).
evidence.methodology: About 100 seconds is the reported duration of the mean stem-potential change, not a nectar refill time. No per-bee success rate or new calculation is presented.
